subject: Physics
title: Alternating Current
summary: How a sinusoidal voltage drives current through a resistor, an inductor, a capacitor and a series LCR combination, why the current can lead or lag the voltage, what resonance and power factor mean, and how a transformer steps voltage up or down. It closes Unit IV with Chapter 6, and the LCR phasor derivation and the transformer are among the most predictable questions in the paper.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit IV (Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents: Chapters 6 and 7) carries 8 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. This chapter typically contributes 4 to 5 of those: one 3-mark or 5-mark question on the series LCR circuit or the transformer, plus one or two 1-mark questions on phase, reactance or power factor.

question_types.note: Peak and rms conversions, which device makes current lead or lag by π/2, how X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> change with frequency, impedance and power factor at resonance, the frequency of a resonant LC pair, and the turns ratio of a transformer.
Zero average power in a pure inductor or capacitor, why a transformer does not work on DC, why a capacitor blocks DC, resonance needing both L and C, and why ac meters read rms values.

Define rms value or power factor; draw the graph of X<sub>L</sub> or X<sub>C</sub> against frequency; identify device X from the phase of its current; a one-step reactance or transformer numerical; what wattless current is.

Show that the average power in a pure inductor or capacitor is zero; a series LCR numerical asking for impedance, current, phase and power; energy losses in a transformer and how each is reduced; a lamp in series with a capacitor or inductor and what happens to its brightness when frequency or the core changes.

Derive the impedance and phase angle of a series LCR circuit from the phasor diagram, state the resonance condition and draw the current–frequency graph; or explain the principle, construction and working of a transformer with the turns-ratio derivation, losses and its role in power transmission, usually with a small numerical attached.
A passage on resonance and radio tuning, on power factor and wattless current, or on a transformer in a transmission line, followed by four one-line or two-step parts.

hot_topics: Series LCR circuit: impedance and phase angle from the phasor diagram, resonance condition ω<sub>0</sub> = 1/√(LC), and the current–frequency curve
Transformer: principle, turns ratio, step-up and step-down, energy losses and their remedies, use in long-distance transmission
AC through a pure inductor and a pure capacitor: phase relation, reactance, graphs of X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> against frequency, zero average power
Power in an ac circuit: P = VI cos φ, power factor, wattless current, and the values of cos φ in the standard cases
rms and peak values: definition, I = i<sub>m</sub>/√2, why ac meters read rms
Numericals on reactance, impedance, current and voltage drops across R, L and C
Identifying an unknown element from the phase of its current and drawing its phasor diagram
Choke coil and why an inductor is preferred to a resistor for limiting ac

sections.heading: 7.1 Introduction
sections.body:
A direct current flows in one direction with a fixed value. An alternating current reverses direction periodically and, in the case we study, varies sinusoidally with time. The household supply in India is an alternating voltage of 220 V at 50 Hz. The word "ac" is used loosely for both alternating current and alternating voltage; the phrase "ac voltage" is standard even though it is redundant.

Why ac and not dc? Three reasons the examiner likes to see. First, ac voltages can be stepped up or down easily and efficiently with a transformer, which is what makes long-distance transmission practical. Second, most electrical energy is generated by ac generators, which are simpler than dc machines. Third, ac can be converted to dc where needed with a rectifier, while the reverse is harder.

The whole chapter rests on one input: a sinusoidal voltage v = vm sin ωt applied to a circuit element, where vm is the amplitude (peak value) and ω = 2πν is the angular frequency. We ask, for each element and then for the series LCR combination, what current flows, how it is related in phase to the voltage, and how much power is absorbed on average. Keep the NCERT symbols: lowercase v and i for instantaneous values, vm and im for peak values, uppercase V and I for rms values. Mixing them up is the commonest source of lost marks in the numericals.

where: angular frequency (rad s<sup>−1</sup>); ν = 50 Hz for the mains

sections.tip: Write the applied voltage as v = v<sub>m</sub> sin ωt at the top of every derivation. Marking schemes award the first step for it.

sections.heading: 7.2 AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor
sections.body:
Connect a resistor R across v = vm sin ωt. By Kirchhoff's loop rule vm sin ωt = iR, so i = (vm/R) sin ωt = im sin ωt with im = vm/R. Ohm's law holds at every instant and the current is in phase with the voltage: both are zero together and peak together. On the graph of v and i against ωt the two sine curves reach their maxima at the same instants; in the phasor diagram the phasors v and i lie along the same line.

The average of a sine over a full cycle is zero, so the average current is zero. That does not mean no energy is dissipated, because Joule heating goes as i2, which is always positive. The instantaneous power is p = i2R = im2R sin2 ωt. Using sin2 ωt = ½(1 − cos 2ωt) and the fact that cos 2ωt averages to zero over a cycle, the average power is P = ½ im2R.

To write this like the dc formula, define the root mean square (rms) or effective current I = √(average of i2) = im/√2 = 0.707 im. Then P = I2R. The rms current is the steady dc current that would produce the same heating in the same resistor in the same time. Similarly V = vm/√2, and V = IR, P = IV = V2/R. The 220 V of the mains is an rms value; the peak is vm = √2 × 220 = 311 V. Ac ammeters and voltmeters read rms values, which is why ac circuit calculations use rms quantities exactly as dc formulas use steady values.

formulas.expr: i = i<sub>m</sub> sin ωt, i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/R

where: average power over a full cycle (W)

sections.tip: If a question says "220 V, 50 Hz" the 220 V is rms. If it says "v = 311 sin 314t" then 311 V is the peak, ν = 314/2π = 50 Hz, and the rms voltage is 220 V.

sections.heading: 7.3 Representation of AC Current and Voltage by Rotating Vectors — Phasors
sections.body:
In an inductor or a capacitor the current is not in phase with the voltage, and adding sinusoids of different phases by algebra is clumsy. The phasor is the tool that makes it easy. A phasor is a vector that rotates anticlockwise about the origin with angular speed ω. Its length is the amplitude of the quantity (vm or im) and its projection on the vertical axis at time t gives the instantaneous value: vm sin ωt for a voltage phasor at angle ωt.

Two quantities with a phase difference φ are represented by two phasors with the angle φ between them; since both rotate at the same ω, the angle between them never changes. For a resistor, the v and i phasors lie along the same direction. For an inductor, the current phasor is π/2 behind the voltage phasor (measured against the sense of rotation). For a capacitor, the current phasor is π/2 ahead.

Because the projections of phasors obey the same addition rules as the phasors themselves, voltages across elements in series can be added as vectors. That is exactly what we do for the LCR circuit in Section 7.6. When the examiner asks for a phasor diagram, draw the reference phasor along the horizontal, mark the angle between the phasors clearly with an arrow showing the sense of rotation, and label each phasor with its peak value. A labelled diagram with the phase angle marked usually carries one full mark on its own.

formulas.expr: v = v<sub>m</sub> sin ωt, i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ)
where: phase of the current relative to the voltage; positive means the current leads

sections.tip: Phasors are a bookkeeping device, not a physical rotating vector in the circuit. State that the projection on the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value.

sections.heading: 7.4 AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor
sections.body:
A pure inductor of inductance L (zero resistance) is connected to v = vm sin ωt. The changing current induces a back emf L(di/dt), and since there is no resistor the loop rule gives v − L(di/dt) = 0, that is di/dt = (vm/L) sin ωt. Integrating, i = −(vm/ωL) cos ωt (the integration constant is zero because the current has no steady part). Since −cos ωt = sin(ωt − π/2),

i = im sin(ωt − π/2), with im = vm/XL and XL = ωL.

XL is the inductive reactance. It has the dimensions of resistance and its SI unit is the ohm, and it plays the role of resistance in limiting the current amplitude. It is directly proportional to frequency: XL = 2πνL, so the graph of XL against ν is a straight line through the origin. At dc (ν = 0) the reactance is zero, so an ideal inductor is a short circuit for dc.

The current lags the voltage by π/2, or one-quarter of a cycle. In the phasor diagram the current phasor is 90° behind the voltage phasor. On the v–i graph the current peaks one quarter period after the voltage does.

Power. The instantaneous power is p = vi = vm sin ωt × im sin(ωt − π/2) = −vmim sin ωt cos ωt = −(vmim/2) sin 2ωt. Over a full cycle the average of sin 2ωt is zero, so the average power is zero. Physically, in one quarter cycle the source builds up the magnetic field of the inductor and in the next quarter the collapsing field returns that energy to the source. This is why a choke coil (an inductor) is used instead of a resistor to reduce the current in a fluorescent-tube circuit: it limits the current without wasting energy as heat.

formulas.expr: i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt − π/2), i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/X<sub>L</sub>

sections.tip: The board's favourite: "a device draws the same current at 200 V dc and less at 200 V ac". That device is an inductor with resistance; use the dc reading for R and the ac reading for Z, then X<sub>L</sub> = √(Z<sup>2</sup> − R<sup>2</sup>).

sections.heading: 7.5 AC Voltage Applied to a Capacitor
sections.body:
A capacitor C is connected to v = vm sin ωt. In a dc circuit a capacitor charges once, current flows only for a moment, and then it blocks the current. With ac the plates are charged, discharged and charged in the opposite sense every half cycle, so a current flows continuously in the wires even though no charge crosses the gap.

At any instant q = Cv = Cvm sin ωt, and i = dq/dt = ωCvm cos ωt. Writing cos ωt = sin(ωt + π/2),

i = im sin(ωt + π/2), with im = vm/XC and XC = 1/ωC.

XC is the capacitive reactance, in ohms. It is inversely proportional to frequency: XC = 1/(2πνC), so the graph of XC against ν is a rectangular hyperbola. At dc, ω → 0 and XC → ∞: the capacitor blocks dc. At high frequency it offers almost no opposition. This is why a lamp in series with a capacitor glows brighter when the frequency of the supply is raised, and does not glow at all on dc.

The current leads the voltage by π/2: the current phasor is 90° ahead of the voltage phasor, and on the graph the current peaks a quarter period before the voltage.

Power. p = vi = vm sin ωt × im sin(ωt + π/2) = vmim sin ωt cos ωt = (vmim/2) sin 2ωt, whose average over a cycle is zero. The capacitor is charged in one quarter cycle and returns the stored electric energy in the next. A pure inductor and a pure capacitor both pass current and both absorb no net power; the difference between them is only the sign of the phase shift.

formulas.expr: i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + π/2), i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/X<sub>C</sub>

sections.tip: Remember the mnemonic ELI the ICE man: in an inductor (L) the emf E leads the current I; in a capacitor (C) the current I leads the emf E.

sections.heading: 7.6 AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit
sections.body:
A resistor R, an inductor L and a capacitor C are in series with v = vm sin ωt. The same current i = im sin(ωt + φ) flows through all three, so the current phasor I is the natural reference. The board asks for the phasor-diagram solution, which goes in four steps.

Step 1: voltage phasors. The voltage across R, VR, is in phase with I and has amplitude imR. The voltage across L, VL, leads I by π/2 and has amplitude imXL. The voltage across C, VC, lags I by π/2 and has amplitude imXC. So VL and VC are opposite to each other, along a line perpendicular to VR.

Step 2: add them. By the loop rule the applied voltage is the phasor sum V = VR + VL + VC. Adding the two collinear ones first gives a phasor of length im|XC − XL| perpendicular to VR; by Pythagoras, vm2 = (imR)2 + (imXC − imXL)2.

Step 3: impedance. Hence im = vm/Z where Z = √(R2 + (XC − XL)2) is the impedance of the circuit, in ohms.

Step 4: phase. From the diagram tan φ = (XC − XL)/R. If XC > XL, φ is positive and the circuit is capacitive: current leads. If XL > XC, φ is negative and the circuit is inductive: current lags. The same result holds for an RL or RC circuit by setting XC or XL to zero.

Resonance. Since XL rises with ω and XC falls, there is one angular frequency at which XL = XC: ω0L = 1/ω0C, so ω0 = 1/√(LC) and ν0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). At this resonant frequency the impedance is minimum, Z = R, the current amplitude is maximum, im = vm/R, and φ = 0, so the circuit behaves as pure resistance. The graph of im against ω is a peak at ω0; a smaller R gives a taller, sharper peak. VL and VC are equal and opposite at resonance and cancel, so the whole applied voltage appears across R; each of VL and VC can individually exceed the source voltage. Resonance needs both an inductor and a capacitor; an RL or RC circuit cannot resonate. Tuning a radio uses exactly this: the capacitor is varied until ω0 matches the frequency of the station wanted, and that signal alone drives a large current.

where: phase by which the current leads the applied voltage (negative means lags)
resonant angular frequency; at resonance Z = R, φ = 0, i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/R

sections.tip: In the 5-mark derivation, draw the phasor diagram with I horizontal, V<sub>R</sub> along it, V<sub>L</sub> up, V<sub>C</sub> down, and the resultant V at angle φ. Missing diagram loses a mark; missing the resonance statement loses another.

sections.heading: 7.7 Power in AC Circuit: The Power Factor
sections.body:
With v = vm sin ωt and i = im sin(ωt + φ) in a series LCR circuit, the instantaneous power is p = vi = vmim sin ωt sin(ωt + φ). Using 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B), p = (vmim/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt + φ)]. The second term averages to zero over a cycle, so the average power is

P = (vmim/2) cos φ = VI cos φ = I2Z cos φ.

P is the true (average) power, VI is the apparent power, and cos φ is the power factor. From the phasor diagram cos φ = R/Z, so P = I2R: on average, only the resistance dissipates energy. Four cases the examiner expects you to state:

  • Pure resistor: φ = 0, cos φ = 1, P = VI. Maximum power.
  • Pure inductor or pure capacitor: φ = ±π/2, cos φ = 0, P = 0. Current flows, but no power is consumed. Such a current is called wattless (or idle) current.
  • Series LCR off resonance: 0 < cos φ = R/Z < 1, P = VI cos φ.
  • Series LCR at resonance: XL = XC, φ = 0, cos φ = 1 and P = VI, maximum.

Wattless current in general: the current I can be resolved into I cos φ in phase with the voltage, which carries all the power, and I sin φ at 90° to the voltage, which carries none. The component I sin φ is the wattless current. A low power factor in a transmission line means a larger current for the same delivered power, so more I2R loss in the cables; that is why supply companies want cos φ close to 1 and add capacitors to inductive loads (motors) to raise it.

formulas.expr: P = VI cos φ = I<sup>2</sup>Z cos φ = I<sup>2</sup>R

where: component of current at 90° to the voltage; consumes no average power

sections.tip: "Power factor 0.5" means cos φ = 0.5, so φ = 60°. Write φ in the answer, not just cos φ; the two-mark question usually asks for the phase difference.

sections.heading: 7.8 Transformers
sections.body:
A transformer changes an alternating voltage from one value to another. Principle: mutual induction. A changing current in one coil induces an emf in a neighbouring coil linked by the same magnetic flux.

Construction: two coils, the primary (Np turns) and the secondary (Ns turns), insulated from each other and wound on a laminated soft-iron core. Either the coils are wound one over the other on one limb, or on separate limbs of a rectangular core. The core is a closed loop so that almost all the flux from the primary links the secondary.

Working and turns ratio: an alternating voltage vp across the primary sets up an alternating flux φ in the core. If every turn of both coils links the same flux, the induced emf per turn is the same, dφ/dt. So the secondary emf is εs = −Ns dφ/dt and the primary back emf is εp = −Np dφ/dt. For an ideal transformer with negligible primary resistance, the applied voltage equals the back emf, giving vs/vp = Ns/Np. If Ns > Np it is a step-up transformer (vs > vp); if Ns < Np it is a step-down transformer. For an ideal transformer there is no loss, so the power input equals the output: ipvp = isvs. Combining, is/ip = vp/vs = Np/Ns. A step-up transformer raises the voltage and lowers the current in the same ratio. It does not create energy.

Energy losses in a real transformer (efficiency is still often above 90%):

  • Flux leakage: not all the primary flux links the secondary. Reduced by winding one coil over the other on a well-designed core.
  • Resistance of the windings: I2R heating in the copper. Reduced by using thick copper wire, especially in the high-current winding.
  • Eddy currents: the changing flux induces currents in the iron core, heating it. Reduced by laminating the core, thin sheets insulated from each other.
  • Hysteresis: the core is magnetised and demagnetised every cycle and warms up. Reduced by using soft iron, which has a narrow hysteresis loop.

Transmission: power P sent along a line of resistance Rc at voltage V carries a current P/V and loses (P/V)2Rc as heat. Raising V by a step-up transformer at the generating station (say 440 V to 132 kV or more) reduces the loss enormously; step-down transformers at substations and near homes bring it back to 220 V. A transformer works only on ac: a steady dc gives constant flux, no dφ/dt, and no secondary voltage.

where: turns in the secondary and primary
less than 1 for a real transformer

sections.tip: For the 5-mark question give all four: principle (mutual induction), a labelled diagram, the turns-ratio derivation with the ideal-transformer power relation, and the four losses with their remedies. Then state why it fails on dc.

key_terms.definition: A current whose magnitude changes continuously with time and whose direction reverses periodically; the standard form is i = i<sub>m</sub> sin ωt.
The maximum value v<sub>m</sub> or i<sub>m</sub> of the alternating voltage or current in a cycle.
The square root of the mean of the square of the current over a full cycle, I = i<sub>m</sub>/√2. It is the steady dc that would produce the same heating in the same resistor in the same time.
A vector rotating anticlockwise at the angular frequency ω whose length is the amplitude and whose vertical projection gives the instantaneous value of a sinusoidal quantity.
The angle φ by which the current leads or lags the applied voltage; zero for a resistor, current lags by π/2 in an inductor and leads by π/2 in a capacitor.
X<sub>L</sub> = ωL, the opposition offered by an inductor to alternating current; it is proportional to frequency and is measured in ohms.
X<sub>C</sub> = 1/ωC, the opposition offered by a capacitor to alternating current; it is inversely proportional to frequency and is measured in ohms.
The effective opposition of a series LCR circuit to alternating current, Z = √(R<sup>2</sup> + (X<sub>C</sub> − X<sub>L</sub>)<sup>2</sup>), so that i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/Z.
The condition X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> in a series LCR circuit, reached at ω<sub>0</sub> = 1/√(LC), at which the impedance is minimum (Z = R) and the current amplitude is maximum.
The cosine of the phase angle between voltage and current, cos φ = R/Z; the average power is P = VI cos φ.
The component I sin φ of the current at 90° to the voltage, which consumes no average power; the whole current in a pure inductor or capacitor is wattless.
An inductor of high inductance and low resistance used to limit alternating current without appreciable loss of energy, for example in fluorescent-tube circuits.

A device based on mutual induction that changes an alternating voltage; v<sub>s</sub>/v<sub>p</sub> = N<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>p</sub>, step-up if N<sub>s</sub> > N<sub>p</sub>, step-down if N<sub>s</sub> < N<sub>p</sub>.
Circulating currents induced in the bulk of a conductor such as a transformer core by a changing magnetic flux; they cause heating and are reduced by laminating the core.
Energy lost as heat each cycle when the core material is magnetised and demagnetised; reduced by using soft iron with a narrow hysteresis loop.

formula_sheet.name: rms values
formula_sheet.note: Mains 220 V is rms; peak = 311 V. Ac meters read rms.

formula_sheet.name: Resistor
formula_sheet.expr: i = (v<sub>m</sub>/R) sin ωt; P = I<sup>2</sup>R = VI
formula_sheet.note: Current in phase with voltage; power factor 1.

formula_sheet.name: Inductor
formula_sheet.expr: X<sub>L</sub> = ωL = 2πνL; i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt − π/2)
formula_sheet.note: Current lags by π/2; X<sub>L</sub> ∝ ν; average power zero.

formula_sheet.name: Capacitor
formula_sheet.note: Current leads by π/2; X<sub>C</sub> ∝ 1/ν; infinite for dc; average power zero.

formula_sheet.name: Series LCR impedance
formula_sheet.expr: Z = √(R<sup>2</sup> + (X<sub>C</sub> − X<sub>L</sub>)<sup>2</sup>); i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/Z; I = V/Z
formula_sheet.note: Set X<sub>C</sub> = 0 for RL, X<sub>L</sub> = 0 for RC.

formula_sheet.name: Phase angle
formula_sheet.expr: tan φ = (X<sub>C</sub> − X<sub>L</sub>)/R; cos φ = R/Z
formula_sheet.note: X<sub>C</sub> > X<sub>L</sub>: current leads; X<sub>L</sub> > X<sub>C</sub>: current lags.

formula_sheet.name: Resonance
formula_sheet.note: Z = R (minimum), I = V/R (maximum), φ = 0, cos φ = 1.

formula_sheet.name: Average power
formula_sheet.note: VI is apparent power; cos φ is the power factor; wattless current = I sin φ.

formula_sheet.name: Voltages across elements
formula_sheet.expr: V<sub>R</sub> = IR, V<sub>L</sub> = IX<sub>L</sub>, V<sub>C</sub> = IX<sub>C</sub>; V = √(V<sub>R</sub><sup>2</sup> + (V<sub>L</sub> − V<sub>C</sub>)<sup>2</sup>)
formula_sheet.note: Never add V<sub>R</sub>, V<sub>L</sub>, V<sub>C</sub> arithmetically.

formula_sheet.name: Transformer
formula_sheet.note: Ideal (lossless) transformer; efficiency = output power / input power.

formula_sheet.name: Transmission loss
formula_sheet.note: Raising the transmission voltage by 10 cuts the line loss by 100.

diagrams.title: Voltage and current graphs and phasor diagrams for R, L and C
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three pairs. For R: v and i sine curves peaking together, and two phasors along the same line. For L: the i curve peaks a quarter cycle after v, and the i phasor is 90° clockwise (behind) the v phasor. For C: the i curve peaks a quarter cycle before v, and the i phasor is 90° ahead. Label ωt on the axis, mark the π/2 shift, and write 'current lags' or 'current leads' under each.

diagrams.title: Phasor diagram of the series LCR circuit
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the current phasor I horizontally. Put V<sub>R</sub> = i<sub>m</sub>R along I, V<sub>L</sub> = i<sub>m</sub>X<sub>L</sub> vertically upward and V<sub>C</sub> = i<sub>m</sub>X<sub>C</sub> vertically downward from the origin. Draw the difference V<sub>C</sub> − V<sub>L</sub> (or V<sub>L</sub> − V<sub>C</sub>) and complete the rectangle to get the resultant V = v<sub>m</sub> at angle φ to I. Label φ and write v<sub>m</sub><sup>2</sup> = (i<sub>m</sub>R)<sup>2</sup> + (i<sub>m</sub>X<sub>C</sub> − i<sub>m</sub>X<sub>L</sub>)<sup>2</sup> beside it.

diagrams.title: Graphs of X<sub>L</sub>, X<sub>C</sub> and Z against frequency, and the resonance curve
diagrams.how_to_draw: On one set of axes with ν along x, draw X<sub>L</sub> as a straight line through the origin and X<sub>C</sub> as a hyperbola falling from high values; mark their crossing at ν<sub>0</sub>. Below it draw i<sub>m</sub> against ω as a single peak at ω<sub>0</sub> = 1/√(LC), with a second taller and narrower peak labelled 'smaller R'. Label i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/R at the peak.

diagrams.title: Step-up transformer
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a rectangular laminated soft-iron core shown as a closed loop. On the left limb draw the primary coil with fewer turns connected to an ac source; on the right limb draw the secondary with more turns connected to the load. Label N<sub>p</sub>, N<sub>s</sub>, v<sub>p</sub>, v<sub>s</sub> and the core, and write N<sub>s</sub> > N<sub>p</sub> for step-up. Show a few flux lines running round the core.

ncert_questions.q: A 100 Ω resistor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz ac supply. (a) What is the rms value of current in the circuit? (b) What is the net power consumed over a full cycle?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The 220 V is the rms voltage. For a pure resistor I = V/R = 220/100 = 2.2 A.

(b) P = VI = 220 × 2.2 = 484 W (or I2R = 4.84 × 100 = 484 W).

ncert_questions.q: (a) The peak voltage of an ac supply is 300 V. What is the rms voltage? (b) The rms value of current in an ac circuit is 10 A. What is the peak current?
A 44 mH inductor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz ac supply. Determine the rms value of the current in the circuit.
A 60 μF capacitor is connected to a 110 V, 60 Hz ac supply. Determine the rms value of the current in the circuit.
In exercises 7.3 and 7.4, what is the net power absorbed by each circuit over a complete cycle? Explain your answer.
ncert_questions.a: Zero in both. In the pure inductor the current lags the voltage by π/2, and in the pure capacitor it leads by π/2. In each case P = VI cos φ with cos(±π/2) = 0. The instantaneous power is p = ±(vmim/2) sin 2ωt, which is positive for one quarter cycle (energy stored in the field) and negative for the next (energy returned to the source), so its average over a full cycle is zero. The current is wattless.

ncert_questions.q: Obtain the resonant frequency ω<sub>r</sub> of a series LCR circuit with L = 2.0 H, C = 32 μF and R = 10 Ω. What is the Q-value of this circuit?
ncert_questions.a:
ωr = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(2.0 × 32 × 10−6) = 1/√(64 × 10−6) = 1/(8 × 10−3) = 125 rad s−1.

Q = ωrL/R = 125 × 2.0/10 = 25.

(The Q-value and sharpness of resonance are no longer in the rationalised syllabus; the resonant-frequency part is what the board can ask.)

ncert_questions.q: A charged 30 μF capacitor is connected to a 27 mH inductor. What is the angular frequency of free oscillations of the circuit?
ncert_questions.a:
ω = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(27 × 10−3 × 30 × 10−6) = 1/√(8.1 × 10−7) = 1/(9 × 10−4) = 1.1 × 103 rad s−1.

(LC oscillations are no longer in the rationalised CBSE syllabus. This question is kept for conceptual practice only — it will not be asked in the board paper.)

ncert_questions.q: Suppose the initial charge on the capacitor in exercise 7.7 is 6 mC. What is the total energy stored in the circuit initially? What is the total energy at a later time?
ncert_questions.a:
Initial energy is all electrical: U = q2/2C = (6 × 10−3)2/(2 × 30 × 10−6) = 36 × 10−6/(60 × 10−6) = 0.6 J.

The circuit has no resistance, so no energy is dissipated. The total energy stays 0.6 J at all later times; it merely oscillates between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the inductor.

(LC oscillations are no longer in the rationalised CBSE syllabus. This question is kept for conceptual practice only — it will not be asked in the board paper.)

ncert_questions.q: A series LCR circuit with R = 20 Ω, L = 1.5 H and C = 35 μF is connected to a variable-frequency 200 V ac supply. When the frequency of the supply equals the natural frequency of the circuit, what is the average power transferred to the circuit in one complete cycle?
ncert_questions.a:
At the natural (resonant) frequency XL = XC, so Z = R = 20 Ω and cos φ = 1.

I = V/R = 200/20 = 10 A.

P = VI cos φ = 200 × 10 × 1 = 2000 W (equivalently I2R = 100 × 20 = 2000 W).

The resonant frequency itself is ω0 = 1/√(1.5 × 35 × 10−6) = 1/√(5.25 × 10−5) = 138 rad s−1, but it is not needed for the power.

ncert_questions.q: A radio can tune over the frequency range of a portion of the MW broadcast band, 800 kHz to 1200 kHz. If its LC circuit has an effective inductance of 200 μH, what must be the range of its variable capacitor?
ncert_questions.a:
At resonance ω = 1/√(LC), so C = 1/(ω2L) = 1/(4π2ν2L).

For ν1 = 800 kHz: ω1 = 2π × 8 × 105 = 5.03 × 106 rad s−1; ω12 = 2.53 × 1013; C1 = 1/(2.53 × 1013 × 2 × 10−4) = 1/(5.06 × 109) = 1.98 × 10−10 F ≈ 198 pF.

For ν2 = 1200 kHz: ω2 = 7.54 × 106 rad s−1; ω22 = 5.69 × 1013; C2 = 1/(5.69 × 1013 × 2 × 10−4) = 1/(1.14 × 1010) = 8.8 × 10−11 F ≈ 88 pF.

The variable capacitor must range from about 88 pF to 198 pF.

ncert_questions.q: A series LCR circuit with L = 5.0 H, C = 80 μF and R = 40 Ω is connected to a variable-frequency 230 V source. (a) Determine the source frequency which drives the circuit in resonance. (b) Obtain the impedance of the circuit and the amplitude of current at the resonating frequency. (c) Determine the rms potential drops across the three elements of the circuit. Show that the potential drop across the LC combination is zero at the resonating frequency.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(5.0 × 80 × 10−6) = 1/√(4 × 10−4) = 1/0.02 = 50 rad s−1 (ν0 = 50/2π = 7.96 Hz).

(b) At resonance Z = R = 40 Ω. I = V/Z = 230/40 = 5.75 A; amplitude im = √2 × 5.75 = 8.13 A.

(c) VR = IR = 5.75 × 40 = 230 V. XL = ω0L = 50 × 5 = 250 Ω, so VL = 5.75 × 250 = 1437.5 V. XC = 1/(ω0C) = 1/(50 × 80 × 10−6) = 250 Ω, so VC = 1437.5 V.

VL and VC are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase (180° apart), so the drop across the LC combination is VL − VC = 0. The entire 230 V appears across R.

pyq.q: The rms value of an alternating voltage is 220 V. Its peak value is nearly
pyq.answer: c

pyq.q: An alternating voltage v = v<sub>m</sub> sin ωt is applied to a device X and the current is i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + π/2). The device X is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The current leads the voltage by π/2, which is the signature of a pure capacitor.

pyq.q: The frequency of an ac source connected to a pure inductor is doubled. The inductive reactance
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: X<sub>L</sub> = 2πνL is directly proportional to frequency.

pyq.q: In a series LCR circuit at resonance, the power factor and the impedance are respectively
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: At resonance X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so Z = R and φ = 0, giving cos φ = 1.

pyq.q: A series LCR circuit has L = 10 mH and C = 1 μF. Its resonant angular frequency is
pyq.answer: c

pyq.q: In a step-up transformer, compared with the primary, the secondary has
options: more turns, higher voltage and larger current
more turns, higher voltage and smaller current
fewer turns, higher voltage and smaller current
more turns, lower voltage and larger current
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: N<sub>s</sub> > N<sub>p</sub> raises the voltage, and with v<sub>p</sub>i<sub>p</sub> = v<sub>s</sub>i<sub>s</sub> the current falls in the same ratio.

pyq.q: A lamp is connected in series with a capacitor to an ac source. If the frequency of the source is increased, the brightness of the lamp
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(2πνC) falls as ν rises, so the impedance falls, the current rises and the lamp glows brighter.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A transformer cannot be used to step up a dc voltage. Reason (R): A transformer works on the principle of mutual induction, which requires a changing magnetic flux.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: A steady dc gives a constant flux, so dφ/dt = 0 and no emf is induced in the secondary. R states exactly why.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The average power consumed by a pure inductor over a complete cycle is zero. Reason (R): The current through a pure inductor is in phase with the applied voltage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is true, but the current in an inductor lags the voltage by π/2; it is this π/2 lag, not being in phase, that makes cos φ = 0.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): An ac ammeter connected in an ac circuit reads the rms value of the current. Reason (R): The average value of an alternating current over a complete cycle is zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because the cycle average is zero, a meter based on the average would read nothing; ac meters use the heating effect, which depends on i<sup>2</sup> and hence on the rms value.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A series RC circuit connected to an ac source can show resonance if the frequency is suitably chosen. Reason (R): Resonance in a series circuit requires the inductive and capacitive reactances to cancel each other.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Without an inductor there is no X<sub>L</sub> to cancel X<sub>C</sub>, so an RC (or RL) circuit cannot resonate; A is false and R is true.

pyq.q: Why is the core of a transformer laminated? Name the loss it reduces and state one other loss in a transformer with its remedy.
pyq.answer:
The changing flux in the core induces eddy currents in the iron, which heat it and waste energy. Laminating the core into thin sheets insulated from each other breaks the paths of the eddy currents and reduces this loss.

One other loss: copper (I2R) loss in the windings, reduced by using thick copper wire. (Also acceptable: hysteresis loss, reduced by using soft iron; flux leakage, reduced by winding one coil over the other.)

pyq.q: Define the rms value of an alternating current. Write its relation with the peak value.
pyq.answer:
The rms (effective) value of an alternating current is that steady direct current which, flowing through a given resistance for a given time, produces the same amount of heat as the alternating current does in the same time. It equals the square root of the mean of i2 over a full cycle.

For i = im sin ωt, Irms = im/√2 = 0.707 im.

pyq.q: Draw graphs showing the variation of (i) inductive reactance and (ii) capacitive reactance with the frequency of the applied ac source.
pyq.answer:
(i) XL = 2πνL: a straight line through the origin, rising with ν. (ii) XC = 1/(2πνC): a rectangular hyperbola, very large at small ν and falling towards zero at large ν.

Label the axes XL (or XC) against ν, and write the equation of each curve next to it. The two curves cross at the resonant frequency if drawn on the same axes.

pyq.q: The power factor of an ac circuit is 0.5. What is the phase difference between the voltage and the current? What is meant by wattless current?
pyq.answer:
cos φ = 0.5, so φ = 60° = π/3. The current and voltage differ in phase by 60°.

Wattless current is the component I sin φ of the current that is 90° out of phase with the voltage; it carries no average power. In a pure inductor or capacitor the entire current is wattless because φ = π/2.

pyq.q: An inductor of 0.1 H is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz ac supply. Calculate the rms current. What is the average power consumed?
pyq.answer:
XL = 2πνL = 2 × 3.14 × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω.

I = V/XL = 220/31.4 = 7.0 A.

Average power = VI cos φ = 0, since φ = π/2 for a pure inductor.

pyq.q: A voltage v = v<sub>m</sub> sin ωt is applied to a pure capacitor. Obtain the expression for the current and show that the average power over a full cycle is zero. Draw the phasor diagram.
pyq.answer:
q = Cv = Cvm sin ωt, so i = dq/dt = ωCvm cos ωt = im sin(ωt + π/2), where im = vm/XC and XC = 1/ωC. The current leads the voltage by π/2.

Instantaneous power p = vi = vmim sin ωt cos ωt = (vmim/2) sin 2ωt. The average of sin 2ωt over one complete cycle is zero, so Pavg = 0. Energy given to the capacitor in one quarter cycle is returned in the next.

Phasor diagram: draw V along the horizontal and I at 90° ahead of it (anticlockwise), both rotating at ω.

pyq.q: A series LCR circuit with R = 30 Ω, X<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω and X<sub>C</sub> = 10 Ω is connected to a 200 V (rms) ac source. Find (i) the impedance, (ii) the rms current, (iii) the power factor and the average power, (iv) the rms voltage across each element.
pyq.answer:
(i) Z = √(R2 + (XL − XC)2) = √(302 + 402) = √2500 = 50 Ω.

(ii) I = V/Z = 200/50 = 4 A.

(iii) cos φ = R/Z = 30/50 = 0.6 (φ = 53°, current lags since XL > XC). P = VI cos φ = 200 × 4 × 0.6 = 480 W. Check: I2R = 16 × 30 = 480 W.

(iv) VR = IR = 120 V, VL = IXL = 200 V, VC = IXC = 40 V. Check: √(1202 + (200 − 40)2) = √(14400 + 25600) = 200 V.

pyq.q: A step-down transformer converts 2200 V to 220 V. The primary has 3000 turns and the secondary delivers 10 A to a load. Assuming the transformer is ideal, find (i) the number of turns in the secondary, (ii) the primary current, (iii) the power drawn from the supply. Why is a step-down transformer used near homes?
pyq.answer:
(i) Ns/Np = vs/vp = 220/2200 = 1/10, so Ns = 300 turns.

(ii) ipvp = isvs: ip = 10 × 220/2200 = 1 A.

(iii) Power = vsis = 220 × 10 = 2200 W, equal to the input vpip = 2200 × 1 = 2200 W for an ideal transformer.

Power is transmitted at high voltage to keep the line current, and hence the I2R loss, small; a step-down transformer near homes brings the voltage to the safe 220 V that appliances are designed for.

pyq.q: A bulb is connected in series with an inductor to an ac source and glows with some brightness. What happens to the brightness if (i) an iron rod is inserted into the inductor, (ii) the frequency of the source is increased, (iii) a capacitor of suitable capacitance is added in series? Give reasons.
pyq.answer:
(i) Inserting an iron rod increases L, so XL = ωL rises, the impedance rises, the current falls and the bulb dims.

(ii) Increasing ν increases XL = 2πνL; the current falls and the bulb dims.

(iii) A capacitor in series introduces XC which subtracts from XL: Z = √(R2 + (XL − XC)2) decreases, the current rises and the bulb glows brighter. If XC = XL (resonance) the brightness is maximum.

pyq.q: (a) A voltage v = v<sub>m</sub> sin ωt is applied to a series LCR circuit. Using the phasor diagram, derive the expression for the impedance of the circuit and the phase difference between the current and the voltage. (b) What is the phase difference between the voltages across the inductor and the capacitor at resonance? (c) An inductor draws 1 A when connected to 200 V dc but only 0.5 A when connected to 200 V, 50 Hz ac. Explain and find its self-inductance.
pyq.answer:
(a) The same current i = im sin(ωt + φ) flows through R, L and C. Voltage phasors: VR = imR in phase with I; VL = imXL leading I by π/2; VC = imXC lagging I by π/2. The applied voltage is the phasor sum V = VR + VL + VC. VL and VC are opposite, so their sum has magnitude im|XC − XL| perpendicular to VR. By Pythagoras, vm2 = (imR)2 + (imXC − imXL)2, so im = vm/Z with Z = √(R2 + (XC − XL)2), the impedance. From the triangle, tan φ = (XC − XL)/R. Draw the phasor diagram with I horizontal, VR along it, VL upward, VC downward and the resultant V at angle φ. Optional but rewarded: Z is minimum (= R) at ω0 = 1/√(LC); sketch Z against ω as a curve falling to R and rising again.

(b) At resonance VL and VC are equal in magnitude and 180° (π) out of phase; they cancel.

(c) On dc only the resistance of the coil limits the current: R = 200/1 = 200 Ω. On ac the inductive reactance adds to the opposition: Z = 200/0.5 = 400 Ω. XL = √(Z2 − R2) = √(160000 − 40000) = √120000 = 346 Ω. L = XL/(2πν) = 346/(2 × 3.14 × 50) = 346/314 = 1.1 H.

pyq.q: (a) Describe, with a labelled diagram, the principle, construction and working of a transformer. Obtain the relation between the secondary and primary voltages in terms of the number of turns, and between the currents for an ideal transformer. (b) State any two sources of energy loss in a transformer and how each is reduced. (c) Why is a transformer of no use with dc?
pyq.answer:
(a) Principle: mutual induction. Construction: two insulated coils, the primary (Np turns) and the secondary (Ns turns), wound on a laminated soft-iron core forming a closed magnetic loop. Working: the alternating voltage vp across the primary produces an alternating flux φ in the core, which links every turn of both coils. The emf induced per turn is dφ/dt, so εs = −Ns dφ/dt and εp = −Np dφ/dt. For an ideal transformer with negligible winding resistance, vp = εp and vs = εs, giving vs/vp = Ns/Np. Step-up if Ns > Np, step-down if Ns < Np. With no losses, input power equals output power: vpip = vsis, so is/ip = Np/Ns. Diagram: closed rectangular core, primary on one limb connected to the ac source, secondary on the other connected to the load, all labelled.

(b) Any two: eddy-current loss in the core, reduced by laminating it; copper (I2R) loss in the windings, reduced by thick wire; hysteresis loss, reduced by a soft-iron core; flux leakage, reduced by winding the coils one over the other.

(c) A steady dc produces a constant flux in the core, so dφ/dt = 0 and no emf is induced in the secondary. The transformer gives no output, and the primary, having low resistance, may overheat.

pyq.q: (a) Explain the term resonance in a series LCR circuit. Obtain the expression for the resonant frequency and draw the graph showing the variation of current amplitude with the angular frequency of the source for two values of R. (b) A series LCR circuit with L = 100 mH, C = 100 μF and R = 10 Ω is connected to a 200 V (rms) variable-frequency source. Find the resonant angular frequency, the current at resonance and the average power absorbed at resonance.
pyq.answer:
(a) In a series LCR circuit the current amplitude is im = vm/√(R2 + (XC − XL)2). As ω increases, XL = ωL rises and XC = 1/ωC falls, so at one frequency they become equal and the impedance is minimum, Z = R. The current is then maximum, im = vm/R, and the current is in phase with the voltage. This is resonance. Condition: ω0L = 1/(ω0C), so ω0 = 1/√(LC) and ν0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). Graph: im against ω is a peak centred at ω0; for smaller R the peak is taller and sharper, for larger R it is lower and broader. Resonance needs both L and C; it is used in tuning a radio.

(b) ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(0.1 × 10−4) = 1/√(10−5) = 1/(3.16 × 10−3) = 316 rad s−1 (ν0 = 50.3 Hz).

At resonance Z = R = 10 Ω, so I = V/R = 200/10 = 20 A.

P = VI cos φ with cos φ = 1: P = 200 × 20 = 4000 W (check: I2R = 400 × 10 = 4000 W).

pyq.q:
A radio receiver has a tuning circuit made of an inductor and a variable capacitor. Signals of many frequencies reach the antenna, but the circuit responds strongly only to the one whose frequency equals its own natural frequency ω0 = 1/√(LC). Turning the tuning knob changes C and hence ω0. The response is sharp if the resistance of the circuit is small.
(i) State the condition for resonance in a series LCR circuit.
(ii) What is the impedance and the phase angle at resonance?
(iii) If L = 1 mH and the circuit must resonate at ω = 106 rad s−1, find the capacitance.
(iv) Why does a circuit containing only R and C not show resonance?
pyq.answer:
(i) XL = XC, that is ωL = 1/ωC, so ω = ω0 = 1/√(LC).

(ii) Z = R, its minimum value, and φ = 0: the current is in phase with the voltage and the power factor is 1.

(iii) C = 1/(ω2L) = 1/((106)2 × 10−3) = 1/(109) = 10−9 F = 1 nF.

(iv) Resonance needs the inductive reactance to cancel the capacitive reactance at some frequency. With no inductor there is no XL, the impedance √(R2 + XC2) simply decreases with frequency and never has a minimum at a particular frequency, so no resonance occurs.

pyq.q:
Electric power is generated at a power station at a few kilovolts and then stepped up to hundreds of kilovolts before being sent along transmission lines to distant cities. Near the city it is stepped down in stages, finally to 220 V for homes. The transformers used are based on mutual induction and are among the most efficient machines ever built, yet they still lose some energy as heat.
(i) Why is the voltage stepped up before transmission?
(ii) A step-up transformer has 100 turns in the primary and 2000 turns in the secondary. If the primary is at 220 V, find the secondary voltage.
(iii) If the transformer in (ii) is ideal and the secondary supplies 0.5 A, find the primary current.
(iv) Name the loss that laminating the core reduces.
pyq.answer:
(i) For a given power P, the line current is I = P/V, and the heat lost in the cables is I2Rc = (P/V)2Rc. Raising V lowers the current and cuts the loss in proportion to 1/V2.

(ii) vs = vp × Ns/Np = 220 × 2000/100 = 4400 V.

(iii) vpip = vsis: ip = 4400 × 0.5/220 = 10 A.

(iv) Eddy-current loss in the core.

practice_mcq.explanation: For dc, ω = 0 and X<sub>C</sub> = 1/ωC is infinite; after the brief charging current, no current flows.

practice_mcq.explanation: Both reactances play the role of resistance, i<sub>m</sub> = v<sub>m</sub>/X, and are measured in ohms.

practice_mcq.explanation: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> is resonance; the reactances cancel and Z = R = 5 Ω.

practice_mcq.explanation: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> gives equal magnitudes IX<sub>L</sub> = IX<sub>C</sub>, and they are 180° apart, so they cancel.

practice_mcq.q: The phase difference between voltage and current in an ac circuit is 60°. If V = 100 V and I = 2 A (rms), the average power is
The power factor of a series LCR circuit is given by
practice_mcq.explanation: From the impedance triangle cos φ = R/Z.

practice_mcq.q: Wattless current flows in a circuit containing
practice_mcq.explanation: The whole current is wattless only when φ = π/2, which needs a pure inductor or pure capacitor.

practice_mcq.q: A choke coil is preferred to a resistor for reducing the current in an ac circuit because it

practice_mcq.explanation: An ideal inductor consumes no average power; a resistor would waste energy as heat.

practice_mcq.q: An ideal transformer has 200 turns in the primary and 50 turns in the secondary. The primary current is 1 A. The secondary current is
practice_mcq.explanation: i<sub>s</sub>/i<sub>p</sub> = N<sub>p</sub>/N<sub>s</sub> = 200/50 = 4, so i<sub>s</sub> = 4 A (step-down: voltage falls, current rises).

practice_mcq.q: The frequency of the instantaneous power dissipated in a resistor connected to a 50 Hz supply is

options: winding the coils on separate limbs
practice_mcq.explanation: Soft iron has a narrow hysteresis loop, so less energy is lost per cycle of magnetisation; lamination is for eddy currents.

common_mistakes: Treating 220 V as the peak value. In every mains problem the quoted voltage is rms; convert with v<sub>m</sub> = √2 V only when the question asks for the peak or gives you an equation like v = 311 sin ωt.

Adding V<sub>R</sub>, V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> arithmetically to get the source voltage. They are phasors at 90°; the correct relation is V<sup>2</sup> = V<sub>R</sub><sup>2</sup> + (V<sub>L</sub> − V<sub>C</sub>)<sup>2</sup>. Examiners deduct the whole numerical for this.

Getting the lead and lag the wrong way round. Current lags in an inductor and leads in a capacitor. Writing the wrong sign in i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt ± π/2) loses the derivation mark and the phasor diagram mark together.

Stating the average power in a pure inductor or capacitor is zero without showing the working. The mark is for p = ±(v<sub>m</sub>i<sub>m</sub>/2) sin 2ωt and the statement that sin 2ωt averages to zero over a cycle.
Forgetting the 2π when converting frequency to angular frequency. X<sub>L</sub> = 2πνL and X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(2πνC); with 50 Hz, ω = 314 rad s<sup>−1</sup>, not 50.
Claiming a transformer increases power. It changes voltage and current in inverse ratio; the output power is at most equal to the input. Also, naming a loss without its remedy scores only half.
Answering 'power factor 0.5' with cos φ = 0.5 and stopping. The question wants φ = 60°; write both.
Using the Q-factor or LC oscillation formulas in a board answer. Sharpness of resonance and LC oscillations are out of the rationalised syllabus; resonance itself and ω<sub>0</sub> = 1/√(LC) are in.
strategy:
This is a short chapter with a fixed set of questions, so prepare it in a single evening and revise it in an hour. Start with the three basic elements. Write out, from memory, the current expression, the reactance, the phase relation, the graph of reactance against frequency and the zero-power proof for the inductor and the capacitor. That is the whole of Sections 7.4 and 7.5 and it feeds every question that follows.

Then learn the series LCR phasor derivation as a four-step routine: voltage phasors, vector addition, impedance by Pythagoras, phase angle from the triangle. Practise drawing the phasor diagram until it takes thirty seconds, and always end with the resonance condition and its consequences (Z = R, current maximum, φ = 0). Follow it with the power expression P = VI cos φ and the four cases of the power factor.

The transformer is a memorised answer: principle, labelled diagram, turns-ratio derivation, the ideal power relation, four losses with remedies, and why it fails on dc. Write it out once in full.

Numericals: do NCERT 7.1 to 7.11 and one LR, one RC and two LCR problems with rms voltages across each element. Keep a small table of the standard numbers: √2 = 1.414, 1/√2 = 0.707, 2π × 50 = 314, and 220 V peak = 311 V.

In the exam, give the 1-mark questions no more than a minute each, and spend the time saved on the phasor diagram and the transformer diagram, which are where full marks are lost by rushing.
revision_checklist: I can write v = v<sub>m</sub> sin ωt and convert peak to rms and back (I = i<sub>m</sub>/√2)
I can derive P = I<sup>2</sup>R for a resistor and explain why ac meters read rms values
I can explain what a phasor is and draw the phasor diagrams for R, L and C
I can derive i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt − π/2) for an inductor and write X<sub>L</sub> = ωL
I can derive i = i<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + π/2) for a capacitor and write X<sub>C</sub> = 1/ωC
I can sketch X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> against frequency and say what happens at dc
